title: 84 Preventing acidosis with bunk management and impacts of grain processing on small-scale, farmer-feeder feedlots
content:
Abstract
Cattle feeding in non-traditional areas usually involves smaller scale, farmer-feeders who grow their own corn for grain and corn silage and feed one group of cattle per year. There is a growing trend for these feeders to feed cattle for the local market, especially since Covid, as there has been an increase in the construction of small-scale meat packing plants. The other group of cattle feeders are former dairy producers who have confinement barns that are adapted to feed cattle. Some of the major challenges these smaller-scale feeders face are the cost of grain processing, lack of steam-flaking capacity, the lack of understanding of the benefits of a uniform grain particle size, and a lack of training in, and knowledge of, bunk management. These part-time cattle feeders often have jobs off the farm, and almost always have other farming operations such as raising row crops and forages for hay. As a result of these competing interests for time and labor, cattle in many areas are still fed using self-feeders resulting in a reduction in feed efficiency and an increase in sub-acute acidosis as the grains are normally relatively finely ground. Increasingly, cattle are fed using feed bunks but are often fed ad libitum with little effort to control feed intake. The emphasis of many of these farmers is adding another stream of income and an emphasis on feed efficiency has not been a primary goal. In addition, having a consumer base of repeat customers is a primary goal, which means that an emphasis on meeting the demands of customers who are willing to pay more for meat products from cattle raised under certain management strategies, such as not using anabolic implants or feed-grade antibiotics, is a bigger driver of management decisions than focusing on optimizing efficiency or average daily gain. In contrast to the larger cattle feeding industry, many of these smaller-scale feedlots are in areas of greater human population, and marketing to the local consumer base is often a critical part of the farm’s overall income. Training of these farmers in management to prevent acidosis, including how to identify acidosis, goes with training in bunk management. In addition, educating producers on nutrition and management to improve marbling is critical, as consumers who are willing to pay a premium for local meat products often demand highly marbled meat products.
